title: Scoped AuthZ Model, SSO Consent Flow, and Audit Evidence Packaging PRD
creator: Asha Patel
description: PRD to define a scoped authorization model and the SSO consent/attribute flow for Private/VPC deployments, plus an operational runbook for packaging audit evidence (logs, assertions, key custody proofs) for customer audits. This doc clarifies scope changes requested by enterprise pilot customers, lists concrete acceptance tests, and defines sign-off owners across PM, Security, Legal, and Engineering. The goal is to enable predictable audit artifacts and reduce time-to-audit for customers using customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and SAML-based SSO.
requirements: Provide SAML 2.0 SSO integration guidance with required attributes (email, sub, groups) and optional attributes mapping for RBAC
Define consent capture pattern for SSO where organization-level consent is required; store consent records for at least 180 days by default
Map SAML assertions to platform RBAC roles; support group-to-role mappings and per-tenant role overrides
Expose audit evidence export: signed SAML assertions, IdP metadata, session traces, and request-level audit logs for a requested date range
KMS/HSM: define key custody model, rotation windows, and escrow procedures; support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and external HSM connectors
Retention & tamper-evidence: immutable append-only audit logs with cryptographic signing and tamper-detection checks
Operational runbook for evidence packaging: standardized ZIP layout, manifest.json, chain of custody checklist, and SRE contact
Backwards compatibility: existing private deployments must accept a non-breaking config rollout and an automated migration guide
APIs for programmatic evidence requests with SLA: request -> prepare -> deliver within configured SLA windows
RBAC admin UX: ability to view/approve consent records and to map IdP groups to Redwood roles in Console
acceptance_criteria: SSO: SAML SSO can be configured in a Private deployment and an end-to-end login with attribute mapping succeeds in >90% of tested IdPs
Consent: Consent records are created, stored and retrievable via Console and API; export shows timestamps, actor, and policy version
Audit export: Evidence package contains signed assertions, a signed manifest, and a tamper-check report; packages can be generated for arbitrary 30-day windows
KMS: Customer-managed key can be attached, rotated on schedule, and key usage events appear in exported evidence with key identifiers
RBAC: Group->role mappings apply consistently across requests; a canary tenant shows no regressions after rollout
SLA: Evidence request lifecycle completes within agreed SLA in 95% of requests in staging
Security review: Threat model and mitigations documented and security sign-off obtained
Legal: Export artifact format and retention meet legal/privacy checklist and legal sign-off is recorded
signoff_checklist: PM acceptance: confirm PRD and acceptance criteria
Security review: formal approval of threat model, tamper-detection, and KMS patterns
Engineering acceptance: implementation plan, performance impact analysis, and test harness ready
Legal review: privacy & export compliance check
SRE/ops: runbook reviewed and playbook validated in staging
Customer Success: pilot customer acceptance test plan and post-migration checklist
Delivery: Documentation artifacts (Console docs, API reference) published
decisions: Default audit retention set to 180 days with configurable tenant override
Evidence package will use a signed manifest (Ed25519) for tamper detection
KMS integration will support envelope encryption with customer key IDs surfaced in exported evidence
Consent records stored as hashed blobs with plaintext available in export only to authorized auditors
RBAC mapping will be group-centric with optional attribute-based rules for advanced tenants
risks: IdP variance: attribute naming differences across customers increase mapping effort
Performance: generating large evidence packages may affect runtime during peak loads without proper throttling
Legal: cross-border export of assertion artifacts may require special handling for some customers
Operational complexity: key escrow and HSM connectors introduce staffing and runbook demands
